title: Get Biggest Three Rhombus Sums in a Grid
spaceBreakdown:
- two prefix arrays dr, dl: m×n ints each → O(m·n)
- set<int> s: capped at 3 entries → O(1)
- not counted: input grid, returned vector
approach: Every rhombus is determined by its center (i,j) and radius k; its border consists of four diagonal segments. Build two prefix-sum arrays along the ↘ and ↙ diagonals so each side's sum is a difference of two entries, making each rhombus sum O(1). Enumerate all centers and radii, keep the three largest distinct sums in a set capped at size 3.
hints: A rhombus border is made of four straight diagonal runs of cells - what if each run's sum could be answered instantly instead of walked cell by cell? The grid is at most 50×50, so even ~50·50·50 rhombus evaluations are fine if each is cheap.

Use prefix sums along the two diagonal directions (↘ and ↙), then each of the four sides is one subtraction. Keep the answers in a set holding at most 3 distinct values. E.g. in Example 2, center (1,1) with radius 1 gives 4+2+6+8 = 20 from four one-subtraction side queries.

```
build dr[i][j] = grid[i][j] + dr[i-1][j-1]      (↘ prefix)
build dl[i][j] = grid[i][j] + dl[i-1][j+1]      (↙ prefix)
for each cell (i,j):
    add grid[i][j] as a radius-0 rhombus
    for k = 1 .. max radius fitting in grid:
        sum = (four side sums via dr/dl differences)
              minus the four corner cells (counted twice)
        insert sum into set, keep only 3 largest distinct
return set in descending order
```

**Single cell** - a 1×1 grid has only the area-0 rhombus.
`Input: [[5]]` → `Expected: [5]`
⚠️ Bug: looping radii from 1 and skipping k = 0 → returns `[]`.

**All equal values** - every rhombus sum collides.
`Input: [[7,7,7]]` → `Expected: [7]`
⚠️ Bug: storing sums without deduplication → returns `[7,7,7]`.

**Area-0 rhombi required** - single cells count as valid rhombus sums.
`Input: [[1,2,3],[4,5,6],[7,8,9]]` → `Expected: [20,9,8]`
⚠️ Bug: only enumerating k ≥ 1 → returns `[20]`.

**Prefix index off the grid** - for center (i,j), radius k, the term dr[i-1][j-k-1] can have j-k-1 = -1.
`Input: [[3,4],[5,6]]` → `Expected: [6,5,4]`
⚠️ Bug: reading dr[i-1][-1] without a bounds guard → wrong sums or runtime error; e.g. center (1,0) side sum becomes 25−3=22 instead of 25 on Example 1's blue rhombus, giving 225 instead of 228.

followUps.q: What if the grid can be up to 1000×1000 - does your approach still work?
followUps.a: Yes, the diagonal-prefix approach scales directly: time becomes O(m·n·min(m,n)) ≈ 10^9 worst case, so you would additionally need the O(1)-per-border trick kept and possibly prune radii, but the same prefix arrays (O(m·n) space) still apply. Brute-force border walking would be ~100× slower and risk TLE.

followUps.q: Return the biggest K distinct rhombus sums instead of three, with K up to 10^5?
followUps.a: Replace the size-3 set with a min-heap of size K plus a hash set for deduplication, or keep the full set of sums and take the top K at the end. Time stays O(m·n·min(m,n)) plus O(S log K) for S distinct sums; space grows to O(K) for the heap.

followUps.q: You are given the grid as a read-only stream row by row and may use O(n) extra memory?
followUps.a: Diagonal prefixes only depend on the previous row, so keep just two rolling rows of ↘ and ↙ prefix sums (O(n) space) and process rhombi whose bottom row has already arrived - a rhombus with center (i,j), radius k is fully known once row i+k is read. Time is unchanged at O(m·n·min(m,n)), space drops to O(n).
